world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.note: Lautu Chin: only comparative Kuki-Chin refs (VanBik 2006, Peterson 2017) on Glottolog; no grammar/phonology of Lautu located.

new_statements.quote: Finally, it is also relevant to note that Lutuv syllables are limited to three types: open syllables (CV), closed syllables ending in a velar nasal (CVN), which can both be collectively referred to as major syllables, and minor syllables (Cə) which occur as part of an iambic “sesquisyllabic” structure (CəCV). Matisoff (1973:86) coined the term sesquisyllabic to describe these “syllable and a half” structures, which are common in many Tibeto-Burman languages. The first syllable in these sesquisyllabic structures is very short. In Lutuv, the nucleus of a minor syllable is always /ə/ [...] As Lutuv is a tonal language, pitch patterns are indicated where possible.
new_statements.citation: Bohnert, Amanda, Kelly Harper Berkson & Sui Hnem Par. 2022. Vowel sounds in Hnaring Lutuv. Indiana Working Papers in South Asian Languages and Cultures 3(1) (IWPSALC Special Volume: Hnaring Lutuv Squibs), 3 pp. Bloomington: Indiana University. doi:10.14434/iwpsalc2022.v3i1.35447
new_statements.locator: sec. 1 'Inventory & description', p. 1 (end) to p. 2 (top), and sec. 2 'Sample words', p. 2 with fn. 1-2 (IWPSALC 3(1), 'Page 1 of 3' - 'Page 2 of 3')
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Lutuv is a tone language (three surface pitches H/M/L, analysis preliminary). Words are monosyllabic major syllables (CV or CVŋ, bimoraic) or sesquisyllables Cə.CV(ŋ) in which the initial minor syllable (monomoraic, always /ə/, 'very short') is the weak member of an iambic pattern, i.e. prominence falls on the final major syllable. No independent word-stress contrast is described; nothing beyond this iambic sesquisyllable remark is said about stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Table 2 marks surface pitch (H/L/M, plus rise/fall on bimoraic rhymes) on sample words; pitch of minor syllables is marked mid (e.g. pakaa [pə̄káá] 'plate').
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, elicited citation forms from one native speaker (co-author Sui Hnem Par, Hnaring village); the authors state their tone analysis is 'in its infancy' and give no statement on word stress as such; the only prominence claim is the 'iambic' characterisation of Cə.CV sesquisyllables (minor syllable short and weak, major syllable strong).
new_statements.identity_note: All first-hand sources describe Hnaring Lutuv, the variety of Hnaring village (southern Lutuv area, Thantlang Township, Chin State), from a single consultant (Sui Hnem Par); Glottolog laut1236 lists no dialect nodes. 'Lutuv' is the community's own name; Glottolog/ISO use 'Lautu'. Lutuv/Lautu (Maraic, South Central/Kuki-Chin) is distinct from Mara [mrh], Zophei [zyp] and Senthang [sez].
